title: Heatstroke: warning signs, first aid and prevention

sources.publisher: U.S. National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (CDC)
sources.title: Heat-related Illnesses

sources.publisher: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
sources.title: Protect Yourself From the Dangers of Extreme Heat
Climate change, heat and health (fact sheet)

facts.text: Heatstroke is the most serious heat-related illness and is a medical emergency.
In heatstroke, the body loses its ability to control its temperature and sweating may stop working.
Signs of heatstroke include confusion, slurred speech, fainting or loss of consciousness, and hot, dry skin or heavy sweating.
Body temperature can rise to dangerous levels within 10 to 15 minutes, and without emergency treatment heatstroke can cause permanent disability or death.
First aid for heatstroke: call emergency services, move the person to a cool place and cool them with cold water or cold wet cloths on the head, neck and armpits.
People should drink plenty of fluids even when they do not feel thirsty.
Older adults are less likely to sense and respond to changes in temperature, so others should check on them.
Never leave children or pets in parked cars, because car temperatures can quickly become deadly.
Loose, lightweight, light-colored clothing and sunscreen help; sunburn slows the skin's ability to release heat.
Avoid hard activity in the hottest part of the day and schedule outdoor exercise for cooler times.
